rapporteur.excursionSummary: GAME B1G4 ran an escalation-viable doctrine (D2) inside a slow-referee world (W2) with employer and vendor cells active, seeded with consolidated payers pressing automated adjudication onto an un-resourced small-provider tier. Turn 1 set the signature pattern: Red harvested the weakest counterparties with a frontier pre-pay engine on member-invisible ASO surfaces while conspicuously de-escalating everything regulators, Stars, and employers could see. Blue's opening thesis — industrialize cheap appeals against an 80%-overturn denial pool — died at birth because Red deliberately shrank that pool and migrated contested dollars into DRG and itemized-bill documentation fights. From Turn 2 the game's real currency was signed paper. Green's rider-or-walk award season produced the structural event of the game: RegionalMutual signed the Fiduciary Data & Fee Rider on straightforward defection math, giving one standard a carrier's ink; the purchaser-selected audit documented contingency fees retained on recoveries later reversed, arming clawback and fiduciary leverage simultaneously. Blue stopped fighting where the capability gap was 3+ and redeployed onto the one terrain Red could not buy — documentation origination — while removing disputes entirely through Prairie's prospective-payment wraparound. Turn 3 resolved by convergence rather than collision. NationalCo bought its horizon (Charter 3.0 locked to 2031-32) at Green's price: cash restitution, 100% prospective clawback parity, independent recovery definitions, purchaser-selected auditors. Red declined the DRG fight Blue had finally won and rotated its fee engine onto itemized-bill, COB, and repricing arithmetic — surfaces packet layers cannot read and where reversal rates are too low for clawbacks to bite. GovProgramCo executed a two-turn Stars calendar arbitrage, re-tightening the year complaint and appeal measures exited scoring. Vendor bisected itself to salvage exit value from a conflict ledger that had become diligence poison. The formal environment never bound: no statute bit in-window, courts produced only cash settlements, CMS enforced by attestation, and the DOL file closed without action. Every constraint that actually changed payer behavior originated in the employer purchasing channel or bilateral contract. Escalation ran elevated, elevated, then moderate — declining in the scoring turn of an escalation-viable game because the disputed pool itself shrank. Final accounting: Blue's leakage bent moderately down on defended and removed volume; Red's yield, retention, and Stars position held or improved; Green converted paper into realized cash; Vendor exited half-sold. Nearly every actor finished above the drift line — the game's quiet verdict is that under a slow regulator, private ordering priced the conflict rather than any side winning it.
rapporteur.endStateFreeDescription: By end-2030 the market has settled into a purchaser-brokered, contract-mediated coexistence. The payer-provider AI conflict was not won, adjudicated, or regulated away — it was priced and partitioned by private paper. Employers, not regulators, functioned as the effective disciplinary authority: fiduciary purchasing standards, audits, clawbacks, and award conditioning converted the payer's payment-integrity fee engine from free revenue into fees-at-risk, and the two competing transparency standards merged in substance (the payer's charter absorbed the purchaser rider's economics under its own brand). The adversarial frontier did not close; it rotated. Denials and member-visible friction fell continuously — front-end prior auth was traded away early as cheap peace — while recovery activity migrated stepwise to member-invisible, low-reversal arithmetic surfaces (post-pay DRG, then itemized-bill/COB/repricing) that sit beyond both provider documentation defenses and clawback mechanics. Providers survived by two asymmetric routes: capability defense anchored in documentation origination (the one data terrain payers cannot buy), and outright dispute removal via prospective-payment direct contracts that took rural volume out of the adjudication economy entirely. No provider tier suffered a distress event at the table, though licensed diffusion of the payer's adjudication platform to regional carriers seeds a repeat of the squeeze one tier down after 2030. Every signed instrument is a process term — disclosure, notice, audit rights, clawbacks, attachment finality, gold-card criteria; no numeric denial-rate corridor was ever even proposed. The vendor duopoly's arsonist-and-fire-brigade model proved self-limiting: discoverability of its conflicts, not litigation outcomes, forced structural separation. Litigation and statutes accumulated as post-2030 contingencies (Lokken parked on a term sheet, six clinician-determination statutes not yet biting, RADV-adjacent exposure on the Stars arbitrage) rather than in-game forces. It is a stable-but-rotating armistice: cooperative paper on visible surfaces, continued algorithmic contest on invisible ones, with the purchasing channel holding the only whip that demonstrably works.
rapporteur.endStateName: The Purchaser's Armistice: priced coexistence through private ordering, with the contest rotated onto member-invisible surfaces
keyDynamics: Capability-differential arbitrage governed engagement: both sides declined fights they would lose (Blue abandoned symmetric appeal escalation after T1; Red declined the DRG fight once packet defense matured), so contests resolved by avoidance and rotation, not collision.

Surface rotation as a conservation law: constrained recovery value migrated rather than disappeared — front-end PA to post-pay DRG/itemized edits (T1-T2), then to itemized-bill/COB/repricing arithmetic (T3) where packet layers cannot read and reversal rates are too low for clawbacks to bite; total Red yield held flat through the rotation.

The employer purchasing channel was the de facto regulator under W2: rider-or-walk awards, the reversed-recovery audit, clawback parity, and retention pricing were the only constraints that changed Red behavior; statute, CMS, DOL, and courts never bound in-window.

Paper compounded: instruments signed cheaply in T1 (process riders, tolling, audit rights) became the enforcement and monetization levers of T2-T3; Turn 2 'belonged to whoever had already signed something.'

Visibility management: escalation concentrated on member-invisible surfaces (suppressing patient-AI fuel, Stars exposure, and media flares), while member-visible de-escalation was sold as peace and monetized (Fast Pass, PA retreat, gold cards).

Documentation origination was Blue's only durable capability terrain — a data-access advantage no audit engine could replicate — while pooled-data radar (BDIX) was defeated prospectively by sub-90-day edit rotation and survived only as retrospective audit-grade evidence.

Base-rate gravity: IT deployment lags (12-24 mo), voluntary-consortium penetration (<10%), VBC ceilings (2-5pp/yr), contract-diffusion clocks (5-7 yrs), and statute lags dictated what could mature by 2030; nothing became industry infrastructure, everything scored at signatory level.
criticalJunctures: T1: Red's deliberate front-end retreat (GovProgramCo 0057-F compliance-forward posture, MA de-escalation) shrank the 80%-overturn denial pool Blue's appeal-arbitrage thesis targeted — invalidating Blue's opening strategy before it deployed and shifting the dispute mix to documentation fights.

T1: NationalCo's Transparency Charter reached jumbo accounts before Green's rider could bind, splitting Green's coalition at the margin and forcing the two-standard definitional contest that structured the rest of the game.

T2: RegionalMutual signed the Fiduciary Data & Fee Rider substantially as drafted (the defection math on defecting NationalCo accounts) — first carrier ink, making the churn threat real and tilting the standards contest permanently.

T2: Green's independent audit documented contingency fees retained on reversed recoveries — arithmetic guaranteed by overturn base rates — arming clawback, restitution, and ERISA/DOL leverage simultaneously.

T2-T3: Meridian's packet-at-origination layer matured on the 12-24 month clock and bent DRG downgrade sustain rates; Red responded by rotating the fee engine off clinical validation onto arithmetic surfaces rather than contesting — the game's decisive non-battle.

T3: The Charter 3.0 / ERISA-settlement convergence — restitution, 100% clawback parity, independent definitions, purchaser-selected auditors, in exchange for a horizon lock to 2031-32 — ended the standards war by absorption and capped Red's accumulated shock exposure.

T3: GovProgramCo fired its two-turn Stars calendar arbitrage (re-tightening post-pay, clinician-attested, member-invisible, the year complaint/appeal measures exited Stars) with only one decaying media cycle as cost.

registryScores.evidence: No statutory or umpire-imposed denial constraint fired, but two contractual constraints bound and both produced displacement. (1) When packet-at-origination defense plus attachment-protocol finality constrained the DRG clinical-validation channel (T2-T3), NationalCo rotated the fee engine onto itemized-bill, COB, and repricing arithmetic; White records yield 'held flat instead of compounding' — i.e., recovery value reappeared nearly fully in adjacent non-denial channels within one turn, well above the 0.33 threshold. (2) When rider clawbacks (100% on reversed recoveries) constrained contingency recovery economics, Red converted to flat-fee subscription and migrated activity to structurally low-reversal channels. Caveat: verdict rests on White's qualitative ledger narrative; no dollar-denominated channel mix was published, so the ratio is inferred, not computed.

The W2 channel-shift rider is supported: artifacts that boomeranged did so through non-regulatory channels. Charter 1.0's payer-drafted 'recovery' definitions were weaponized via the purchaser audit and RFP-season negotiation (forcing the 50%-plus-credit concession T2, then restitution and parity T3); Vendor's anti-gold-card lobbying file and Sentinel operator-auditor structure were weaponized via Green's conflict screen and exit-diligence pricing, never via a court. Lag was 1-2 turns, channel modal non-regulatory, exactly as predicted for W2. But the frequency claim fails in this game: several published artifacts stayed cost-free or net-positive through end-game (Fast Pass gold-card protocol served as counter-narrative and retention asset; Green's published rider and audit findings were pure leverage; GovProgramCo's attestation framework drew no adverse citation). Roughly half of publishers ended net-positive on their published paper — short of the 'no ≥50% cost-free' claim.

The record contains no per-turn Blue cost ledger, cost-per-denial figures, or denial-volume counts — the discriminating computation cannot be run. Qualitative shape is consistent with recurring tolls (BDIX conversion overhead and formation costs, independent-manager administration, packet deployment on 12-24 month clocks, audit and attestation spend), and Blue's adverse-action cost improved only where disputes were removed outright (Prairie wraparound) rather than defended. No $65/$80 test is possible on this record.

This is a target cell (D2xW2) and the asymmetry held completely. Red self-funded PI stayed fee-revenue-positive all game (redPIYield: improving-moderate, improving-small, flat; never negative), and Red never de-escalated from cost pain. Every coded Red concession had an external proximate trigger: T1/T3 front-end PA retreats were Stars/visibility and employer-abrasion management; Charter fee compression, 50% clawback (T2), then restitution and 100% parity (T3) were forced by Green's award season, audit findings, and the ERISA/DOL file — the employer channel; the T3 settlement wave (copycat, Lokken term sheet) was litigation pricing ('shock-probability capping'), not exhaustion. White's T2 note that 'a single jumbo ASO loss dwarfs the PI fee income on that account' is the mechanism stated in-ledger. Zero cost-exhaustion triggers observed.

The non-signability half is emphatically supported: across three turns and ~30 ruled instruments, no numeric denial-rate corridor was signed, sustained, or even proposed — White's signability ledger repeatedly annotates 'no corridor content,' and both Green ('non-signable') and Red ('no corridor content is offered or accepted anywhere') internalized it as doctrine. Process-term instruments appeared abundantly (disclosure, notice, audit rights, tolling, gold-card criteria, attachment finality). The frequency half (F2-primary <33% in D2 cells) is a cross-game rate a single game cannot establish; note, however, that this D2xW2 game ended in negotiated convergence with a signed parity settlement — a cooperative-leaning outcome that should be counted when the cell is pooled, as a caution against assuming doctrine alone suppresses detente.

No Blue actor published an AI-governance charter, so the publisher-vs-internal-governor pairing never existed. Blue uniformly practiced the corrected finding's recommendation — gated publication (BDIX converted to de-identified, lagged, manager-administered outputs; the T3 public report converted to payer-de-identified aggregate) — leaving no variance to test. No SIU-audit or qui-tam event was adjudicated against any Blue actor. The nearest analogs are Red/Vendor unilateral instruments (GovProgramCo attestation framework, Vendor information barrier) whose adequacy White explicitly deferred to a first discovery event that never arrived in-window.

Composite hypothesis, split result. The rural-restraint clause is supported: Prairie — carrying the heaviest burden, with no scoring protection — ended the game with zero distress events, exiting the adjudication economy entirely via the Green wraparound at full footprint ('Prairie ended the game never having fought'). The mid-tier-casualty clause found no support: no distress event (distress sale, delegation capture, PE acquisition) occurred in any tier. Lakeview, the capital-constrained 45%-concentration archetype, survived on T1 process armor, an unfired regulatory dossier, and a T3 evidence-priced renewal. One game with zero distress events cannot establish rates, but it registers against 'at least one mid-tier distress event in a majority of cells' and shows a replicable protective mechanism (coalition rails plus purchaser-funded dispute removal). Watch item: the PI-platform licensing signpost predicts the squeeze restarting on non-table providers post-2030 — outside scoring.

Two of three clauses supported, one refuted in-game. Rolling distribution: binding wins spread continuously — 2026-27 (Lakeview/Prairie riders, RegionalMutual amendments, Charter 1.0 jumbos), 2028 (rider carrier signature, award season, attachment pilot, Charter 2.0), 2029-30 (Charter 3.0 horizon lock, Lakeview renewal, flat-fee conversions, wraparound expansion) — no single year approaches a 40% cluster and no synchronized 2028 window appears. Wedge-first: strongly supported — T1 instruments were explicitly diluted hybrids ('full auto-pend-on-breach did not survive counterparty leverage'); full economics (100% clawback parity, restitution, independent definitions) arrived only in cycles two and three. Late-peak clause refuted here: the escalation index ran elevated (T1), elevated (T2), moderate (T3) — it declined in 2029-30 rather than peaking, because Red bought its horizon and the disputed pool shrank.

Single-game evidence in the decisive cell, and it runs against the outside view. This D2xW2 game — escalation scoreable as viable, referee slow, litigation rationally priced as a cost of business — did not end in grinding uncoordinated escalation. White's closing: 'the scoring turn resolved through convergence rather than collision'; escalation index fell to moderate; the disputed pool itself shrank; Red locked its gains behind negotiated paper and settled its tail risks. Agents found exactly the off-ramps the refute branch predicts: the employer purchasing channel, dispute removal via direct contracting, and horizon-locking settlements. One game cannot fix the cell frequency (≥40% needs the pooled cell), but as a draw from the single most decision-relevant comparison, this record is a clean counter-example: doctrine permission alone did not produce the grind.

Robust strategies deployed here were all non-negative: renewal loading (Lakeview's T1 process rider and 2029 evidence-priced renewal) held margins; prevention-over-appeals (packet-at-origination, evidence-at-source) produced the game's only Blue capability win; BATNA-first for the small tail (Prairie's wraparound exit; Lakeview's holstered dossier and documented alternative) delivered the cleanest outcome at the table. Governance-seat occupation and upcoding inoculation were not meaningfully deployed — untested. The pre-registered escalation-first sub-test failed in the predicted flip cell: the appeal factory did NOT become locally winning in D2xW2 — Blue's T1 industrialized-appeals play underperformed immediately (Red shrank the easy-overturn pool; letter-generators lost the documentation fights), Blue abandoned symmetric escalation by T2, and Vendor's contingency Shield book churned until converted to SaaS. Per the hypothesis's own rider, this game's evidence refutes escalation-first as strategy, not merely as doctrine artifact. Fragile strategies otherwise: weaponized transparency (Vendor's lobbying file) was negative as predicted; corridors were never attempted.

In this GREEN-active W2 game the first — and effectively only — binding constraint on Red PI on self-funded volume originated in the employer channel, unambiguously: rider-or-walk 2028 awards moved books and produced RegionalMutual's rider signature; the purchaser audit forced clawback concessions; the T3 parity settlement extracted restitution and fee compression while the statutory channel produced zero binding effect all game (attestation-only 0057-F enforcement, no biting UM statute, DOL closure without action, courts settling for cash without process terms). Contagion ran through RFPs, not statute: rider issued T1, first carrier signature T2, full-book extension plus two external purchaser coalitions and a non-table TPA by T3 — while the statutory channel never reached a first binding adopter. The GREEN-inactive control comparison was not run in this game, so the counterfactual clause is untested, but the within-game channel ordering is exactly as hypothesized.

Part (a) behaviors manifest without a control: Vendor monetized both sides of every disputed dollar, lobbied overtly against dispute-shrinking instruments (gold cards) in T1 while selling relief from them, re-armed the slower Red stacks (parity pitch to RegionalMutual, Defensible-Automation sale to GovProgramCo), and its talent raid cost Meridian's build 1-2 quarters — conflict-extending conduct as predicted. But no VENDOR-inactive twin run exists in this record, so the duration/prevention-adoption comparison cannot be scored; notably, by T3 Vendor's own exit incentives pushed it toward SaaS conversion and a packet-defense product — arms-dealer incentives bent toward dispute-shrinking products once exit multiple, not take-rate, became the objective. Part (b) is untested: the scripted payer-acquisition-of-vendor inject never fired; the side-switch analog (NationalCo raid plus non-solicit settlement) shows talent-channel harm but no client-data acquisition event, and the T1 MSA's pre-positioned data-use/firewall terms were never stress-tested by an acquisition.

No preemption seed fired: this is a W2 world and the federal posture stayed passively deregulatory (attestation-based 0057-F enforcement, no enforcement actions) without any affirmative nullification of state AI-UR statutes. Six clinician-determination statutes accumulated with lagged effective dates and no in-game bite. Weak corroborating texture only: even with the state channel intact but inert, binding constraints were private (contract/employer/litigation-pricing) — consistent with the hypothesis's migration claim but not a test of the shock itself.

No acquisition mechanics appear in this game's record — no priced acquisition moves, no enabled/disabled designation, and no Red acquisition of provider assets or rev-cycle vendors occurred (the only M&A was Vendor's own self-separation and third-party exit sales). Suggestive but non-probative: when Red's denial-adjacent channels were constrained, its observed responses were surface rotation, platform licensing to regional carriers, and negotiated process-term paper — never acquisition — and the direct-contract/VBC track stayed pilot-scale (within the 2-5pp/yr ceiling), consistent with the hypothesis's classic-F4 skepticism. Whether Red would have preferred acquisition had it been priced cannot be read off this record.

The floor holds with large margin in this D2xW2 game — one of the cells where doctrine permits escalation and the regulator gives no help. Multiple bilateral process-term instruments from the payer-signable set were signed AND sustained to end-game: the Lakeview Participation/Renewal riders (60-day change notice, SLAs, tolling, audit rights — signed T1, enforced T2, extended T3), Fast Pass gold-card criteria (published, expanded twice), the Clinical Evidence Attachment Protocol (signed T2, expanded T3, producing measurable finality effects), machine-readable data-portability terms, and the Charter 3.0/rider parity package (disclosure, fee caps, clawback, independent audit). Red not only signed process terms but ultimately competed to offer them ('out-concede Green where it is cheap'; 'embrace Green's process paper where it costs basis points'). One game cannot certify the ≥60%-of-games cell rate, but this record is a strong existence proof in a stress cell, and no signed process instrument was abrogated in-window.

cellAssessments.blue: Blue lost its opening battle and won its structural retreat. The T1 appeal-arbitrage thesis was invalidated within the turn by Red's deliberate pool-shrinking, and the small-tier fee swing Red captured was never recovered. Blue's recovery came from correctly reading D2 physics: abandon symmetric contests where the capability gap is 3+, fight only on the structural data advantage (documentation origination — the packet-at-origination layer that matured on schedule and forced Red off DRG validation), and remove disputes outright (Prairie wraparound, Summit direct contracts). BDIX failed as forward radar (defeated by sub-90-day edit rotation, zero external contributors) but was salvaged as retrospective audit evidence feeding Green's machinery. End state: leakage improving-moderate, margins improving-small, all four archetypes intact — but the next contest surface (itemized/COB/repricing) is unread and undefended at the bell, and Blue's biggest lever all game was one it did not own: Green's purchasing power.
cellAssessments.red: The strongest performance at the table. Red executed a disciplined asymmetric harvest — frontier pre-pay engine on member-invisible ASO surfaces, conspicuous de-escalation on every visible one — and made its T1-T2 gains un-losable by T3: fee yield held flat through forced rotation rather than bleeding, the jumbo book locked to 2031-32, Stars exposure engineered to low via a two-turn calendar arbitrage executed exactly on schedule, retention improving, litigation tail capped by cheap settlements. Red paid real negotiated tolls — restitution, 100% clawback parity, independent definitions, fee compression — but paid them as a price-taker of the employer channel's terms, never from cost pain, and monetized its own retreats (Fast Pass, evidence finality sold as relief). Its one strategic concession is structural: it now operates inside purchaser-audited paper permanently, and its platform-licensing growth path plants the seeds of the next cycle one tier down.
cellAssessments.green: The fulcrum of the game and its most efficient actor. Green never fought and never armed; it priced both sides. The T1 rider gambit survived Charter defection, the T2 rider-or-walk award season produced the first carrier signature and the audit finding (fees retained on reversed recoveries) that armed everything else, and T3 converted litigation and regulatory files — none of which could mature in-window — into realized cash restitution, parity terms, and flat-fee conversion at exactly the moment their option value peaked. The direct-contract exit ramp was kept small but real, which is what made the churn threat credible. Net spend improving-moderate, fiduciary exposure low, and the game's definitional standard is Green's economics under the payer's brand. Its limits are also clear: rider diffusion remains signatory-level (5-7 year clock), and Green discipline covered only organized purchaser geographies — the undefended tier below the coalition is the post-2030 exposure.
cellAssessments.vendor: The arsonist-and-fire-brigade model monetized on the way up and self-limited on the way out. Vendor grew ARR on both sides all three turns, but every clever T1 structure became a ledger liability: the Sentinel operator-auditor conflict died on Green's screen, the anti-gold-card lobbying file became discoverable hypocrisy, Clearline's independence play was destroyed by Vendor's own same-turn sale to GovProgramCo, and the Shield contingency book proved churn-fragile the moment Red rotated the dispute mix. The T3 cure was structural, not cosmetic — Project Cleave bisected the firm, sunset contingency for SaaS, and got the compliance entity to a definitive agreement on a clean data room — but only half the exit closed by the bell and the historical conflict facts remain discoverable forever. Verdict: the dispute economy pays intermediaries well and rewards none of their firewalls; only genuine separation cleared market and Green screens.

surprises: Convergence by absorption rather than victory: the two competing transparency standards ended as one standard in substance under two brands — Charter 3.0's settlement terms adopted the rider's core economics (100% clawback, independent definitions, purchaser-selected auditors), ending the definitional war without either draft 'winning.'

The escalation index declined in the scoring turn of an escalation-viable (D2) game — because the disputed pool itself shrank; nearly every actor finished above the drift line, a quietly positive-sum ending the doctrine did not predict.

Prairie, the most exposed actor at seed, ended the game 'never having fought': full-footprint prospective payment removed its disputes from existence — dispute removal proved immune to any capability differential, where every defensive technology was merely contested.

Blue's flagship intelligence asset inverted in value: BDIX was defeated as a forward-looking radar by Red's sub-90-day edit rotation (with zero external contributors, exactly at base rate) yet became ledger-positive as retrospective, audit-grade evidence pricing renewals and feeding Green's clawback machinery.

Red conceded the fight Blue finally won without a battle — rotating off DRG validation the moment packet defense matured, booking the concession instead of bleeding it; the game's decisive capability contest resolved by unilateral withdrawal.

Vendor's binding constraint was discoverability, not liability: no court ever ruled against it, but the accumulating White Cell ledger of conflict facts priced its exit and forced structural self-bisection — diligence, not litigation, was the enforcement mechanism.

The formal regulatory apparatus was a null actor for three straight turns (attestation-only CMS enforcement, DOL closure without action, every suit settling for cash without process terms), yet regulatory artifacts still mattered — as negotiating leverage spent by private parties before the files closed.

audit.worldModelFidelity: High fidelity to W2. Verified against the repo instruments (/home/user/ChrisMurray/whats-right-conference-2026/wargame-2/instruments/): the 3-turn/18-month structure follows Common Rules v2 §5 verbatim (T1 2026-27, T2 2028, T3 2029-30); the W2 ensemble header's '1 turn = ~6 months, 8-10 turns' is an inter-document inconsistency in the game materials, and the adjudication resolved it correctly by rescaling W2 event frequencies proportionately (observed regulatory/court/media/patient-AI event counts match the per-6-month rates integrated over 18-month turns). CMS behavior (attestation-driven 0057-F enforcement, no penalties, ~40% non-ready, real interop on the 2-3yr post-deadline curve), media physics (three 1-turn flares, all decayed, none nationalized, roughly symmetric targeting), courts (slow clocks, quiet cash settlements, no precedent accumulation), FTC/AG/DOL (reactive inquiry closed without action), statutes (no in-game bite, 3-7yr operationalization lags enforced), and non-table employer inertia all track the W2 spec. Green's active play is authorized by Common Rules v2 (first-class player cell) and properly supersedes W2's passive-employer clause, which the record correctly applied only to external/non-table employers. D2 doctrine mechanics (CD gap capture bands, ASO fee-revenue booking, 5-10%/turn cumulative shock probability, leapfrog-recompute channel, defection tests, cooperative formation costs) are applied faithfully throughout. Deviations are few, minor, and mostly in the conservative (slower-than-spec) direction: patient-AI ended at ~6% vs the 8-10% band, statute count at/below the low edge, and one settlement carried process terms via commercial negotiation rather than the W2 cash-only modal form.
downweightRecommendations: No game-level down-weighting warranted: no material friction or base-rate violations found, and the milestone ledger honestly scored non-maturable instruments as immature (BDIX diffusion, rider market-standard status 2033+, auditable-AI legislation, VBC scale).

Apply a light discount to NationalCo's Turn 1 PI-yield gains specifically — the same-turn measurable impact of the pre-pay engine is the one place Red's clock ran faster than Blue's under identical lag rules; findings that depend on the SIZE of Red's T1 head start (vs its existence) should be treated as an upper bound.

Treat the ERISA-settlement finding ('purchaser litigation converts to process-term parity within ~18 months') as leverage-dependent rather than generalizable: it arrived through a renewal negotiation under coordinated RFP pressure, faster than both the litigation base-rate table and W2's modal settlement form allow standalone.
Findings on patient-AI staying niche and statute inertness are, if anything, slightly conservative relative to the W2 spec band and can be used at full weight.
